headline_en: Experience and impressions of a trip to Germany
summary_en: Travelogue by an Italy-based Bangladeshi (founding president of Europe Bangladesh Press Club) of a short trip to Frankfurt, Germany, in December 2023. It includes remarks that restaurant work is commonly available in Frankfurt with higher pay but higher costs and a housing shortage, that Germany has few migrants because entry is hard and laws strict, and that Bangladeshi students in Germany get permanent residence and citizenship after studying and finding jobs. It gives estimates of Bangladeshis in Italy and Germany.

facts.statement: The writer, an Italy-based Bangladeshi, says that in Frankfurt, Germany, living is expensive and there is a housing shortage, but work is commonly available, especially in the restaurant sector, where Bangladeshi and other migrants work.

According to the writer, pay in Germany (Frankfurt) is much higher than in other European countries, though costs are also much higher; a cappuccino costs 1 euro in Italy but 3 euros 50 cents in Germany.
The writer says Germany has few migrants compared with other European countries because it is not easy to enter and because of strict laws.
Unofficially more than 200,000 Bangladeshis live in Italy; by the count of the Bangladesh Embassy in Rome there are about 160,000, and the number has since risen.
facts.source_in_article: the writer; Bangladesh Embassy in Rome

facts.statement: According to Habib Ullah Bahar, a Germany-based Bangladeshi human rights activist and journalist, there are about 40,000 Bangladeshis in Germany, plus a large number of Bangladeshi students.

According to Habib Ullah Bahar, Bangladeshi students in Germany, after finishing their studies and getting a job, are getting the chance of permanent residence and citizenship; many Bangladeshi students are staying permanently in Germany by this route. Bahar himself was a student and now works as a financial accountant in a private company, living in Mainz.

The writer notes that from Frankfurt's international train station (Hauptbahnhof) one can easily travel to Austria, Switzerland, France and other European countries, so travellers use Germany as a transit point.

Per a statistic cited by the writer, Frankfurt's population in 2024 was about 800,529 (printed as '8 lakh 529'), up from 532,413 in 1950 and up 4,092 in the past year; it hosts migrants from Italy, Turkey, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria and other countries.
facts.source_in_article: a statistic cited by the writer

people_cases.who: Habib Ullah Bahar, Bangladeshi journalist and human rights activist
people_cases.what_happened: Came to Germany as a student, finished studies and now works as a financial accountant at a private company

headline_en: EU countries can be a big market for Bangladeshi migrants: finance minister
summary_en: Finance Minister Abul Hassan Mahmood Ali told the Economic Reporters Forum in Dhaka on 5 February 2024 that EU countries could be a big market for Bangladeshi migrants, but only if they stay legally. He said Bangladesh does not want any of its people to live irregularly in the EU and that EU officials told him about USD 1 billion a year comes from Italy and Bangladeshis are in demand there.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Finance Minister Abul Hassan Mahmood Ali said on 5 February 2024 that EU countries could be a big market for sending Bangladeshi migrants, but Bangladeshis must stay there legally; if a legal opportunity exists, Europe will accept those who want to go or live there.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Abul Hassan Mahmood Ali

facts.statement: The finance minister said the government does not want any Bangladeshi to stay irregularly in EU countries, that irregular migrants have no dignity and cannot work properly, and that they must be brought into a framework; he said he told an EU official at a conference in Mongolia that Bangladesh wants to solve this.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Abul Hassan Mahmood Ali

facts.statement: According to EU information relayed by the finance minister after meeting EU Ambassador Charles Whiteley in Dhaka, about USD 1 billion (100 crore US dollars) a year comes to Bangladesh from Italy, and Bangladeshis are in high demand in Italy.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister, citing the EU side

headline_en: Chance to enrol in HSC while living in South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait and Italy
summary_en: Bangladesh Open University's Open School opened admission for its overseas (NISH-2) HSC programme for the 2024-25 session (2024 batch). Bangladeshi migrants or people of Bangladeshi origin in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, South Korea and Italy can enrol through the Bangladesh embassy, with an online application deadline of 20 February 2024 and fees of USD 180 and USD 165.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Open University (BOU) Open School opened admission to its overseas (Bohi-Bangladesh, NISH-2) HSC programme for the 2024-25 session (2024 batch) for Bangladeshi migrants working or living in, or people of Bangladeshi origin in, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, South Korea and Italy, through the Bangladesh embassy in each country. Streams: humanities and business studies.

The online application deadline for BOU's overseas HSC programme (2024 batch) was 20 February 2024; admission is completed at the Bangladesh embassy in the country concerned after applying online and paying the fee.

Online application for BOU's overseas HSC programme is at forms.gle/i5yYws4GyotjtQaDA; contacts: the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Italy, South Korea or UAE; Dean, Open School, BOU: dean.os@bou.ac.bd; International Academic Program Wing, BOU: iapw@bou.ac.bd; website bou.ac.bd.

Eligibility for BOU's overseas HSC programme: passed SSC/Dakhil/O-level or a government-recognised equivalent, and be a Bangladeshi citizen migrant in Saudi Arabia/Qatar/Kuwait/UAE/South Korea/Italy or of Bangladeshi origin.
BOU overseas HSC programme fees: USD 180 for first-year admission and USD 165 for the second year, each paid at the time of that year's admission.
Registration for BOU's overseas HSC programme lasts a minimum of 2 years and maximum of 5 years; it cannot be completed in under two years, and no student may sit exams after five final examinations.

Documents needed for BOU's overseas HSC programme: one photo, copies of the JSC/JDC/Class 8 or equivalent pass certificate and marksheet, a copy of the passport and a copy of the national ID card (if any).

facts.source_in_article: Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development

facts.statement: The new Saudi caps on service-provider costs for domestic worker recruitment (15 January 2024): Philippines 14,700 riyals, Sri Lanka 13,800, Bangladesh 11,750, Kenya 9,000, Uganda 8,300, Ethiopia 5,900.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development

facts.statement: The Saudi ministry said the newly set maximum cost limits for domestic worker recruitment must not be exceeded; it said the aim is to raise service quality, improve the labour market and make Saudi Arabia attractive to domestic workers.

headline_en: Expatriate Bangladeshi sentenced to death by Kuwaiti court for killing friend who posted his wife's photos on Facebook
summary_en: A Kuwaiti criminal court on Tuesday (about 3 November 2026) sentenced an unnamed expatriate Bangladeshi to death for the premeditated murder of a friend. Prosecutors said the friend had posted private photos of the man's wife on Facebook and refused to remove them; the accused waited outside the victim's workplace with a knife and stabbed him repeatedly. The accused confessed in court.

facts.statement: A Kuwaiti criminal court on Tuesday (about 3 November 2026) found an expatriate Bangladeshi guilty of intentional, premeditated murder of a friend and sentenced him to death.

According to Kuwaiti prosecutors, the victim, a friend, had shared private photos of the Bangladeshi man's wife on Facebook (taken without permission during an earlier visit) and refused repeated requests to delete them, posting more instead; the accused waited with a knife outside the victim's workplace and stabbed him repeatedly in the head and body, killing him. The accused confessed in court.
facts.source_in_article: Kuwaiti prosecutors; the accused's statement in court

headline_en: Lured with high-paying jobs in China, 12 women held captive and abused for trafficking
summary_en: Special Response Battalion (SRB-1) rescued 12 women in Dhaka on Monday (about 26 October 2026) who had been brought from Chattogram with promises of high-paying jobs in China. They were confined in a house, physically and mentally abused and pushed towards immoral work, with plans to traffic them abroad without valid travel papers or passports. The women were handed to families; a case was being prepared and the accused were being sought.

facts.statement: Twelve women were lured from Chattogram to Dhaka with promises of high-paying jobs and other benefits in China, then forcibly confined in a house, physically and mentally abused and offered inducements to 'immoral work'; the plan was to traffic them abroad without valid travel documents or passports.
facts.source_in_article: Special Response Battalion (SRB) press release, citing the rescued women

facts.statement: On Monday (about 26 October 2026) SRB-1 rescued two missing women from the Zamzam Tower area in Uttara West police station area around 3 pm, acting on a missing-person general diary (GD) at Bayezid Bostami police station, Chattogram; based on their information, 10 more women were rescued from the Bhatara area by 1 am.
The 12 rescued women were handed to their families; SRB said a case was being filed at the relevant police station and operations to arrest the accused were ongoing.

headline_en: What lies behind youth protests and violence across Italy; Bangladeshi expatriates worried too
summary_en: Youth-led protests over cost of living, housing, education and government policy spread across Italy after violent protests on 17 October 2026, with fresh protests on 24 October in Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna, Florence and other cities. Many Bangladeshis in Italy run fruit shops, minimarkets and restaurants, and unrest poses a risk of losses; the article found no reliable information that any Bangladeshi-owned shop was attacked or any Bangladeshi was hurt. More protests were announced for 30 October and 20 November.

facts.statement: After violent protests on 17 October 2026, new protests were held on Saturday 24 October 2026 in Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna, Florence and other Italian cities, with clashes, tear gas and water cannon but less looting than the week before; in Bologna at least 19 protesters were injured, and in Turin about 4,000 marched against militarisation, with 2 arrested and 25 charged.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; local emergency health service for Bologna figure

facts.statement: According to Italy's public security department, 4,292 people were identified over the nationwide protests, violence and looting; 371 were taken to police offices (110 minors and 69 foreign nationals), 9 arrested and 87 charged. Nationalities of the 69 foreigners were not published, so whether any Bangladeshis were among them could not be confirmed.

A significant share of Bangladeshis living in Italy are in fruit shops, minimarkets, restaurants and other small businesses; the reporter says shop closures, fewer customers or disrupted goods transport from unrest risk financial losses, especially for fruit and food businesses.

As of 26 October 2026 there was no reliable information that any Bangladeshi-owned shop in Italy had been directly attacked or that any Bangladeshi was injured in the protests, nor any estimate of Bangladeshi traders' losses, nor of organised Bangladeshi participation.

On 24 October 2026 some shops in Milan closed early and some businesses in Trieste boarded up windows and closed temporarily for fear of violence; soldiers were also deployed for security in central Milan.

Organisers of the anti-militarisation movement in Turin announced another street protest for a general strike on 30 October 2026, and student organisations in Italy and the UK planned action on 20 November 2026 against rising education costs.
Fuel price rises linked to the Middle East conflict raised transport costs in Italy; truck drivers' blockades disrupted goods transport in some areas, with possible effects on food prices.

headline_en: Shops of expatriate Bangladeshis also vandalised and looted in France; traders fearful
summary_en: During cost-of-living protests in France the previous week, several businesses of Bangladeshi expatriates in Paris were vandalised and looted, including one trader's phone-accessories shop with about 90,000 euros of goods. Bangladeshi money-transfer outlet operators, food-delivery workers and undocumented day labourers described fear and police document checks. The article lists French government support for damaged businesses, areas of Paris to avoid on Saturday 24 October 2026, the advice to carry proof of legal status, and the penalty for buying or selling looted goods.

facts.statement: During cost-of-living protests in France the week before 23 October 2026, several businesses of expatriate Bangladeshis in Paris were damaged; according to Paris city authorities, 451 shops in Paris alone were vandalised in the violence of 17 and 18 October (count up to 21 October), and the French government said several thousand businesses were damaged nationwide.

A Bangladeshi expatriate trader in Paris named Hasan said his mobile phone accessories and electronics shop was vandalised and looted during the protests, losing all its goods worth about 90,000 euros.

Bangladeshis running small outlets of money transfer firms such as Ria and MoneyGram in Paris fear attacks if street violence resumes, saying such financial outlets have in the past been looted more during protests.
Monir Hossain, a Bangladeshi food-delivery worker in Paris, said the protest-related standstill made deliveries very difficult and workers constantly fear for their safety.

A Bangladeshi day-wage worker in Paris without regular legal papers said strict police presence and document checks everywhere made it hard to go out to work; the article says risk to undocumented expatriates has increased.

French government support for businesses hit by the violence includes the state covering partial unemployment allowance for workers under certain conditions, deferral of tax and social contribution payments, interest-free loans of up to 50,000 euros, and a special fund for eligible small businesses.

The French Federation of Commerce Associations began collecting information on damaged businesses and arranging help; the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Paris and Ile-de-France is helping damaged businesses prepare insurance papers, compensation claims and administrative support.

For the Saturday 24 October 2026 protests, the French government announced deployment of about 70,000 police and gendarmes nationwide; the Louvre, Musee d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais were closed that day.

Paris authorities advised caution moving around central Paris, especially Bastille, Republique, Nation and Les Halles; those who must go out for work should check public transport updates and police instructions before travelling, avoid protest centres and large crowds unless essential, and foreigners living in France should carry proof of their legal papers.

Under the French penal code, buying, keeping or selling stolen or crime-derived goods (such as goods looted during protests) is a serious offence punishable by up to five years in prison and a fine of up to 375,000 euros.

As of 23 October 2026 there was no officially confirmed overall count of damaged Bangladeshi businesses in France; Elan Khan Chowdhury, owner of Union Mart in Paris, said trade had stalled and traders feared for shop security.

On Friday (about 23 October 2026) a shooting in Trappes and La Verriere in western Paris region killed one and injured four; anti-terror authorities were investigating and any link to the protests was unconfirmed.

headline_en: If you want to go abroad for higher education with a low CGPA...
summary_en: Advice piece for students with a low CGPA wanting to study abroad: match universities to results, check minimum requirements, use work experience, research and a strong SOP, and consider foundation, pre-master's or pathway programmes. It says some universities accept proof of English-medium instruction instead of IELTS, but visa and scholarship language rules may differ, and warns against deciding from 'no IELTS / low CGPA' advertisements. Wahid Zaman of consultancy AHZ is quoted.

facts.statement: Students with a low CGPA wanting to study abroad should look for countries, universities and courses matching their results and check minimum entry requirements on the university website; some institutions may relax CGPA requirements or consider alternatives, but admission should not be assumed without meeting minimum requirements.

To offset weak grades, applicants can show relevant work experience, professional training, research, a good portfolio or subject skills, plus a strong statement of purpose (SOP), recommendation letters and a clear future plan.

Many universities require IELTS or TOEFL, but not all; some accept proof that previous study was in English (MOI certificate), an alternative language test, or their own assessment; requirements vary by university and programme.

Wahid Zaman, Country Manager (Bangladesh) of study-abroad consultancy AHZ, advised checking the conditions, tuition fees and progression requirements of pathway or pre-master's programmes, confirming with the university whether an MOI certificate or other test is accepted instead of IELTS, and checking admission and visa requirements separately.

Students who cannot meet direct-entry requirements can look for foundation, pre-master's or pathway programmes that lead to the main course, or conditional admission and preparatory courses at some universities; these are not available in every country, university or level, so eligibility, extra cost, duration and progression conditions should be checked first.

Students should not decide based on advertisements promising admission without IELTS or with low CGPA; they should check the university's recognition, course quality, tuition, scholarship conditions and the language requirement for the visa, because a university accepting an alternative language qualification may still face different visa or scholarship requirements.

headline_en: Australia sharply tightens immigration policy; Bangladeshi students anxious
summary_en: On Thursday 17 September 2026 Australia's Home Affairs and Immigration Minister Tony Burke outlined new visa restrictions: curbing 'visa hopping' by international students, limiting students bringing family, adding a 'no further stay' condition to all tourist visas, stronger removal of overstayers, a lottery for second- and third-year Working Holiday visas, and cutting net migration to 245,000 in 2026-27. Students protested and Bangladeshi students in Sydney voiced fears about their future.

facts.statement: Australian Home Affairs and Immigration Minister Tony Burke said on 17 September 2026 at the National Press Club in Canberra that annual net overseas migration will be cut to 245,000 in financial year 2026-27, with a target of 225,000 a year in later years.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, net migration in the year to March 2026 fell to 292,100, lower than a year earlier and the lowest since mid-2022.

Australia's new policy (announced 17 September 2026) imposes strict restrictions on 'visa hopping', meaning international students enrolling in low-quality courses after finishing higher education or repeatedly changing visas; Bangladeshi students say the chance to move from one course or visa to another is being closed.

Under Australia's new rules, international students' ability to bring family members will no longer be expanded and is being limited; exemptions apply to those already studying in Australia, to applicants from Pacific and Southeast Asian countries, and PhD students can bring their families.
Australia is adding a 'no further stay' condition to all tourist (visitor) visas, which in effect closes the option of going to Australia as a tourist and then applying for another visa there.
Australia is strengthening surveillance and legal measures to make people whose visas have expired leave quickly.

A lottery will be introduced for approval of second- and third-year Working Holiday visas in agriculture and services in Australia; skilled migration will be prioritised in shortage sectors such as construction, healthcare and agriculture.
Australia's new policy gives immigration officers special powers to quickly cancel visas and deport migrants involved in violence against children, family violence and hate crimes.

On 17 September 2026 thousands of international university and high school students boycotted classes and protested in Sydney's Hyde Park, Melbourne and Brisbane against the cuts; universities warned the international education sector could be badly hurt.

A Bangladeshi student living in Denham Court, Sydney, said students paid huge tuition fees to study legally, but frequent rule changes and closing of course/visa switching leave their future very uncertain; a student in Lakemba said temporary-visa holders may face having to return home at any time.

headline_en: Ticket bought to return home, two Saudi expatriates die on the way to the airport
summary_en: Abdul Karim, returning home after about three years in Saudi Arabia, and neighbour Khalid Ahmad, both from Lamar Taluk village in Kanaighat, Sylhet, were killed in a road accident at Al-Khurma on the way from Taif to Jeddah airport on 7 September 2026; four died in total and Karim's son was injured. The article notes earlier road deaths of Kanaighat migrants in Qatar (June) and Saudi Arabia (July).

facts.statement: At about 2:30 pm local time on Monday 7 September 2026, a vehicle travelling from Taif to Jeddah crashed in the Al-Khurma area of Saudi Arabia, killing four people including Bangladeshi expatriates Abdul Karim and Khalid Ahmad of Lamar Taluk village, Kanaighat upazila, Sylhet; the other two dead were unidentified. Abdul Karim's son Mohammad Ali was seriously injured (a broken arm).
facts.source_in_article: local sources; Dakshin Banigram UP chairman Lokman Uddin

facts.statement: Abdul Karim had bought a ticket to return to Bangladesh after about three years in Saudi Arabia; his son Mohammad Ali and neighbour Khalid Ahmad, also expatriates, were driving him to Jeddah airport.
In June 2026 five expatriates from Kanaighat upazila, Sylhet, died in a road accident in Qatar; in July 2026 another Kanaighat expatriate died in a road accident in Saudi Arabia.

headline_en: Proposal to cut visas for international students and their families in Australia worries Bangladeshi expatriates
summary_en: Australian politicians are debating curbs on international student enrolments and family visas amid a housing crisis. One Nation's Pauline Hanson wants to end spouses and family accompanying students, the Coalition wants enrolment limits, and the Labor government's cap bill was blocked in the Senate, though it has already tightened the Genuine Student test, minimum English scores and required bank funds. Bangladeshis in Sydney expressed concern.

facts.statement: Australia's Labor government has already brought in new conditions for international students: a stronger 'Genuine Student' test, higher minimum English scores and a higher amount of funds that must be shown in the bank.
The Labor government's legislation to cap international student numbers was blocked in the upper house (Senate) of Australia's parliament, as of August 2026.

Pauline Hanson, leader of the far-right One Nation party, called for completely ending the right of international students' spouses or family members to come with them, saying students who want family with them should study online from home; the opposition Coalition is calling for limits on student enrolment to prioritise local jobs and skills.

Sydney businessman Zahirul Islam said sudden restrictions on families would push good students to other countries; Tanzina Rahman, a student at a Sydney university, said denying students their spouses would multiply mental stress.

headline_en: Applications open for Germany's DAAD Young Ambassador Programme, Bangladeshis eligible
summary_en: DAAD opened applications for its Young Ambassador Programme 2027 for nationals of India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and Sri Lanka who have studied, researched or taken part in an academic programme in Germany. Ambassadors inform prospective students about German universities, scholarships and funding over two semesters after a mandatory training workshop in November 2026. Deadline 30 September 2026; age under 32 on 1 January 2027.

facts.statement: Germany's DAAD opened applications for its Young Ambassador Programme 2027, a network of alumni who inform people interested in studying in Germany about German universities, scholarships, research and funding; the programme lasts two semesters and starts with a mandatory training workshop on German higher education, research and DAAD scholarships and funding.

Eligibility for the DAAD Young Ambassador Programme 2027: citizen of India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal or Sri Lanka; experience of studying, research or an academic programme in Germany (current students in Germany may also apply); under 32 on 1 January 2027; ready to attend the training workshop in November 2026; eligibility must be checked online before applying. Deadline 30 September 2026.

headline_en: CAA in force in West Bengal; Suvendu announces return of 'illegal' Bangladeshis
summary_en: On 20 May 2026 West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari announced the CAA in force in the state, so all who entered India after 31 December 2024 are deemed illegal. State police will arrest and detain infiltrators not covered by the CAA and hand them to the BSF, which will hand them to Bangladesh's BGB ('detect, delete, deport'). Muslims from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan are not covered by the CAA. He also began handing land to the BSF for border fencing.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 20 May 2026 West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari declared India's 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) in effect in West Bengal; as a result everyone who entered India after 31 December 2024 is to be considered illegal.

The CAA covers seven religious communities; Muslims from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan are not covered. After a 2024 amendment, covered people entering by 31 December 2024 (instead of 31 December 2014) are legally treated as citizens, but this does not apply to Muslims from Pakistan, Afghanistan or Bangladesh. Adhikari said police may not harass covered people who arrived by 31 December 2024.

Adhikari said people not covered by the CAA are illegal infiltrators who will be directly arrested and detained by West Bengal state police and handed to India's Border Security Force (BSF), which will arrange their deportation by handing them to Bangladesh's border force BGB ('detect, delete, deport'); the order applies at all police stations along West Bengal's border, and the police chief and home secretary have been informed.

According to Adhikari, the Indian government sent West Bengal a directive on 14 May 2025 (signed by Under Secretary Pratap Singh Rawat) to hand illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators directly to the BSF, which the previous state government did not act on.

India's border with Bangladesh is 4,000 km, 2,200 km of it with West Bengal, of which 1,600 km is fenced and about 600 km is not; West Bengal began handing land to the BSF to secure a first 27 km stretch for fencing.

headline_en: Mother faints on hearing her sons are ill, unaware none of the four is alive
summary_en: Four brothers from Bandarabazar Para, Lalanagar union, Rangunia, Chattogram, all working as drivers in Oman, died together on Wednesday night (13 May 2026), apparently from gas poisoning inside their car; their bodies were found in the car outside a hospital in Muladdah. The eldest had gone to Oman 10-12 years earlier on heavy loans and brought his brothers. Efforts to repatriate the bodies were under way with help from the upazila administration.

facts.statement: Four Bangladeshi brothers, Muhammad Rashed (40), Muhammad Shahed (35), Muhammad Siraj (28) and Muhammad Shahid (24), of Bandarabazar Para, Lalanagar union, Rangunia, Chattogram, died on Wednesday night (13 May 2026) in Oman; they had phoned their mother saying they had difficulty breathing in the car and were going to hospital, and about half an hour after contact was lost their bodies were recovered from the car in front of a hospital in the Muladdah area. Relatives believe gas released inside the car poisoned them.

Muhammad Rashed went to Oman 10-12 years earlier after borrowing heavily, worked as a labourer, then obtained a driving licence and became a driver for a sheikh; he later brought three younger brothers to Oman and arranged the same driver jobs for them, and the family built a two-storey house.
Efforts were under way to bring the four brothers' bodies home from Oman; Rangunia Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Nazmul Hasan said the upazila administration is assisting the repatriation process.
facts.source_in_article: UP member Amir Hossain; UNO Md Nazmul Hasan
